definition: Innuendo means an indirect hint that implies something damaging.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word innuendo. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know innuendo should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her congratulations arrived wrapped in innuendo: 'Amazing what some people accomplish when the head judge is a family friend.'
A hint merely points somewhere without saying it; an innuendo points at somebody, and the somewhere it points is always unflattering.
A smear is louder than innuendo: innuendo damages through one deniable hint, while a smear is an open campaign of ugly claims.

A dig is an informal jab — a quick, teasing remark aimed at someone, usually delivered openly enough that everyone catches it. An innuendo works under cover: the damaging suggestion is planted indirectly, never quite said, so its maker can deny meaning anything at all.

An aspersion is a remark that attacks someone's honesty or reputation, classically in the phrase 'to cast aspersions,' and it can be made openly and plainly. An innuendo inflicts the same damage sideways: the charge is only implied, wrapped in innocent-sounding words, and stays deniable.
a direct charge, stated openly where it can be answered
a plain, public statement

Innuendo is a fossilized piece of legal Latin: the nod-root inside it (nuere) built no other everyday English words, so nothing in your vocabulary shares it. Remember the picture instead—an innuendo is a nod toward something too ugly to say aloud.
Innuendo means an indirect hint that implies something damaging.
Nobody on the team accused Dev of anything.

There was only innuendo: 'Funny how the equipment fund came up short the same season somebody's got new cleats.' The remark named no one and claimed nothing—yet by Friday half the locker room was glancing at Dev's feet.
Innuendo does its damage while staying deniable: an accusation can be tested and answered, but an innuendo never quite says the thing, so there is nothing to disprove and no one to confront.
Innuendo is the noun for the damaging hint itself; insinuate, its verb partner in this unit, names the act of planting one.
Use innuendo when reporting or judging the tactic—'a campaign of innuendo'—and keep plain hint for suggestions that carry no sting.

The review of Marion Vale's fourth novel never made a single accusation.
It only 'wondered' -- how one writer could produce so polished a book so quickly, and how much her famous editor had contributed to the shaping of its chapters.
Each sentence, read alone, was blameless praise.
Read together, they left an innuendo hanging over the book: that Vale had not really written it.
Vale could not answer the charge, because no charge had been made; objecting would mean saying the ugly thing aloud herself.
Sales held, but invitations thinned, and for two seasons the question followed her from festival to festival.
